The 20th Century was a time of mass migration and economic development, especially for those in the urban working class. At the same time, industrialisation brought great changes to European society as well as the modern world. For example, an increased role for women and the rise of male-dominated professions meant that many workers were expected to take on a larger share of the workforce than they had been before. The result was that the majority of people began to work in jobs where they did not traditionally have been occupied by men. This led to widespread social exclusion which in turn led to inequality.
In this book, we explore how these social factors contributed to the emergence of new forms of labour, including the ways in which certain occupations became more open or more diverse, while others became increasingly exclusive and less popular. We also look at why some occupations such as farming, manufacturing, architecture and crafts were increasingly considered ‘women’s work’. In addition, we examine how other occupations such as medicine and engineering developed under the influence of developments in technology and science. Finally, we see how we can use our knowledge of the history of English language literature to write about everyday life in England during the 19th century

Kowalski works with the University of Miami Coral Reef Lab to study how reef conditions affect coral health and evolution.
A recent research article in PLOS ONE examined the relationship between high and low light levels and bleaching events that were observed during 2013-2015. Using a combination of satellite imagery and aerial observations from multiple sensors including chlorophyll a and b (Chl), researchers determined that most corals experienced bleaching events during this time. They also looked at how changes in ambient light levels impacted on the rate of coral bleaching.
In addition to increasing light exposure during coral bleaching, there was a significant increase in temperature of coral reefs as well as an increased number of dead corals. This study shows that bleaching events can have a profound impact on coral ecosystems and contribute to ecosystem change.
